newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICAN CLOTHING INDUSTRY SAID CONSOLIDATING.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICAN CLOTHING INDUSTRY SAID CONSOLIDATING.

text.p: South Africa's battered clothing industry was heading for a year of consolidation before moving back onto a long-term growth trend, Clothing Federation of South Africa economist Paul Theron said.
In his latest review in Clothing Industry News, Theron said future growth in the domestic market would largely depend on the extent to which government could implement its new economic strategy.

"On the other hand, export-led growth in the short term will be dependent on a stable or depreciating rand and the view taken by the international community on the implementation of that strategy," Theron said.
In the longer term, export growth would be linked to the ability of the government to secure improved access to specific markets such as the European Union and the U.S. on a bilateral basis.
Theron said the production volume index showed that the downturn in the clothing industry started showing signs of levelling out towards the end of 1996.

"Bearing in mind that the index is, in real terms, de-seasonalised and smoothed, it would appear that the industry could be in for a year of consolidation, taking into account the general prospects for the South African economy," he said.
Job losses in the industry also began to level out in the second half of 1996 but it was unlikely that there would be much in the way of job creation in the formal sector.
"The pressure on firms continues, particularly in KwaZulu-Natal," he said.
Firms in the Western Cape were, however, showing a slight increase in employment probably because they were larger and catered for the up-market sector.
Clothing imports exceeded exports in 1996, but this trend was not likely to continue because of the depreciation of the rand.

"But the volatility of the rand will make it difficult for the industry to successfully penetrate the export market on a long term sustainable basis, especially with export incentives being phased out," Theron said.
